problem-formulation.title: Problem Formulation
problem-formulation.lead: Every evolutionary run is shaped by two choices made before the loop can improve anything: what counts as a better outcome, and what form a candidate is allowed to take.
problem-formulation.noteTitle: Two independent parts of the search problem
problem-formulation.noteCopy: The objective defines success; the search space defines the candidates the system can generate. They constrain one another, but they are not the same design choice.

dimensions.title: Optimization objective
dimensions.question: What does better mean?

options.name: Single-objective
options.description: Assign each candidate one scalar score and search for the highest-scoring solution.

options.name: Multi-objective
options.description: Optimize competing criteria together; the result is often a set of trade-offs rather than one winner.

options.name: Quality-diversity
options.description: Seek high quality while also keeping solutions across distinct behavior niches.

dimensions.note: A quality-diversity objective values both performance and coverage of behavior space.

dimensions.title: Search-space representation
dimensions.question: What is being evolved?

options.name: Code
options.description: Executable programs, heuristics, or algorithmic components are the candidate solutions.

options.name: Code templates + parameters
options.description: The system evolves a template while a separate procedure tunes its parameters.

options.name: Workflow structures
options.description: Candidates describe prompts, policies, workflows, or broader optimization-system designs.

dimensions.note: The representation determines what the generator can change and what validity constraints it must obey.

problem-formulation.flowNote: Objectives score candidates; evaluation is the process that obtains those scores.

population.title: Population & Archives
population.lead: The population marks the current search frontier. Archives preserve selected high-value solutions and histories for reuse.
population.noteCopy: Structure, elite retention, and population replacement answer different questions; they are not one flat list of alternatives.

dimensions.title: Population structures
dimensions.question: How are candidates organized?

options.name: Single-individual
options.description: One incumbent is iteratively refined; temporary candidates may still be compared.

options.name: Flat multi-individual
options.description: A shared candidate pool retains alternatives, often with score-based ordering.

options.name: Island-structured
options.description: Subpopulations evolve locally and exchange candidates through migration or reseeding.

options.name: Tree-structured
options.description: Parent-child relations preserve branching lineages and search trajectories.

dimensions.note: Tree structure is an additional organizational layer: it can coexist with flat populations or islands.

dimensions.title: Elite archives
dimensions.question: Which strong solutions are preserved?

options.name: Single-elite
options.description: Keep one current best candidate as the incumbent or best-so-far solution.

options.name: Multi-elite
options.description: Retain several high-performing candidates in a ranked or bounded archive.

options.name: Quality-diversity
options.description: Preserve elites across distinct niches or descriptor-defined cells.

dimensions.note: An elite archive is a logical structure distinct from the main population, even when implementations overlap.

dimensions.title: Replacement mechanisms
dimensions.question: How does retained search history change?

options.name: Incremental insertion
options.description: Add candidates or trajectory records while allowing the reusable pool to grow.

options.name: Elitist replacement
options.description: Admit stronger candidates under top-k or cell-wise archive criteria.

options.name: Generational replacement
options.description: Build a new candidate batch and replace the previous population as a generation.

dimensions.note: Replacement governs updates over time; it does not specify the population's structure or archive type.

population.flowNote: A population stores reusable search state; parent selection decides which parts are exposed next.

parent-selection.title: Parent Selection
parent-selection.lead: A search history may contain many candidates, but only a few can inform the next generation step. Selection determines which prior solutions, references, or records are brought forward.
parent-selection.noteTitle: Selection includes both what is reused and how the choice is controlled
parent-selection.noteCopy: The selected object may be an editable parent or an auxiliary reference. A system can use different rules for these roles, or switch rules as search conditions change.

dimensions.title: Selection mechanisms
dimensions.question: What signal guides retrieval?

options.name: Uniform
options.description: Choose without an explicit preference for candidate quality, preserving broad exploration.

options.name: Score-based
options.description: Use raw fitness or objective magnitude to favor stronger candidates.

options.name: Rank-based
options.description: Use relative ordering or elite membership without relying on score scale.

options.name: Search-statistic-based
options.description: Use uncertainty, visit history, frontier potential, or learned search utility.

options.name: Structure-based
options.description: Use lineage, tree position, island membership, or neighborhood relations.

options.name: Evaluator-metadata-based
options.description: Retrieve candidates using failures, diagnostics, counterexamples, or verifier records.

options.name: Semantic-similarity-based
options.description: Retrieve past candidates or trajectories relevant to the current query or context.

dimensions.note: These signals can select main parents, auxiliary references, or both.

dimensions.title: Selection control
dimensions.question: When does a rule apply?

options.name: Mode-controlled
options.description: Switch selection rules with the search mode, such as exploration versus exploitation.

options.name: Object-specific
options.description: Assign different rules to editable parents, inspiration examples, or retrieved histories.

dimensions.note: Control policy is separate from the selection signal itself: one describes when a mechanism is used.

parent-selection.flowNote: Not every retrieved solution is a genealogical parent; some serve only as contextual evidence.

candidate-generation.title: Candidate Generation
candidate-generation.lead: After reusable parents are chosen, the generator determines how a new candidate relates to them: no parent, a broad rewrite, a local edit, or a synthesis across parents.
candidate-generation.noteTitle: Generation mechanism and mechanism selection are separate
candidate-generation.noteCopy: The first describes how an offspring is formed. The second describes how a system chooses among available generation mechanisms during its run.

dimensions.title: Generation mechanisms
dimensions.question: How is an offspring formed?

options.name: From-scratch generation
options.description: Propose a candidate from task context or retrieved knowledge without editing a parent.

options.name: Large-scale modification
options.description: Use a parent as a starting point but allow broad changes to its algorithm or structure.

options.name: Localized modification
options.description: Constrain changes to patches, diffs, or explicitly marked regions of a parent.

options.name: Multi-parent fusion
options.description: Combine complementary information from multiple parents into one offspring.

dimensions.note: The mechanism determines effective parent count and how much continuity is preserved.

dimensions.title: Mechanism selection
dimensions.question: How is the operator chosen?

options.name: Fixed
options.description: Use a predefined operator, probability mix, or pipeline throughout the run.

options.name: Scheduled
options.description: Assign different mechanisms to predefined stages of the search.

options.name: Adaptive
options.description: Update mechanism choice online using observed progress or operator outcomes.

dimensions.note: Adaptive policies react to search feedback; schedules rely on stages set in advance.

candidate-generation.flowNote: Retrieved examples can guide generation without becoming genealogical parents.

prompt-builder.title: Prompt Builder
prompt-builder.lead: The prompt builder turns task constraints, selected candidates, references, and feedback into the input that conditions model behavior at each search step.
prompt-builder.noteTitle: Prompt structures reflect the role they serve
prompt-builder.noteCopy: Candidate generation, reflection or meta-guidance, and workflow coordination have different goals, so their prompt structures should not be collapsed into one checklist.

dimensions.title: Candidate-generation prompts
dimensions.question: What guides the proposed solution?

options.name: Task description
options.description: State the optimization target, task role, and evaluation requirements.

options.name: Code interface & response format
options.description: Specify inputs, outputs, editable regions, and the required form of the response.

options.name: Artifact & auxiliary context
options.description: Provide the editable parent plus optional examples, histories, hardware, or profiler data.

options.name: Constraints & guidance
options.description: Add feasibility rules, permitted tools, design priorities, or directional instructions.

dimensions.note: The current artifact is the editable target; auxiliary context informs it without necessarily being edited.

dimensions.title: Reflective & meta-guidance
dimensions.question: What intermediate reasoning is requested?

options.name: Target artifact
options.description: Identify the solution, comparison, or search behavior to analyze.

options.name: Evidence
options.description: Supply traces, logs, evaluation outcomes, or prior attempts that ground the analysis.

options.name: Analysis request
options.description: Ask for diagnosis of current results or guidance for future search directions.

options.name: Structured response
options.description: Constrain the output to actionable feedback, ratings, or recommendations.

dimensions.note: Reflection diagnoses a candidate or outcome; meta-guidance recommends how search should proceed.

dimensions.title: Coordination-oriented prompts
dimensions.question: How are roles and work coordinated?

options.name: Routing & dispatch
options.description: Direct information or subtasks to the component responsible for the next action.

options.name: Persistent state
options.description: Carry shared progress or workflow context across specialized roles.

options.name: Interaction protocol
options.description: Organize how agents or system components exchange intermediate results.

dimensions.note: These prompts are usually described by workflow function rather than a single reusable template.

prompt-builder.flowNote: Prompt structure is the interface between search state and semantic generation.

foundation-models.title: Foundation Models
foundation-models.lead: Once context is assembled, the system must decide which model or models perform search tasks and whether their roles stay fixed or change as the run unfolds.
foundation-models.noteTitle: Model count and model assignment answer different questions
foundation-models.noteCopy: A multi-model system may use fixed role assignments or dynamically route work. The number of models alone does not describe how model calls are allocated.

dimensions.title: Model setting
dimensions.question: How many models participate?

options.name: Single-model
options.description: Use one foundation model across the optimization pipeline, keeping behavior easier to attribute.

options.name: Multi-model
options.description: Combine models with different capability, cost, or specialization profiles.

dimensions.note: A single model can still use different inference settings for different tasks.

dimensions.title: Multi-model assignment
dimensions.question: How are model roles allocated?

options.name: Static assignment
options.description: Bind models to fixed roles or a fixed probability mixture throughout the run.

options.name: Dynamic assignment
options.description: Route calls or update model usage in response to stage, uncertainty, or observed progress.

dimensions.note: Dynamic assignment can adapt model capability or cost to the current search need, with added control complexity.

foundation-models.flowNote: Model assignment governs who performs a call; prompts govern what that call is asked to do.

candidate-evaluation.title: Candidate Evaluation
candidate-evaluation.lead: Evaluation returns evidence about a candidate's quality. That evidence may be a direct score, comparative judgment, additional diagnostics, or the result of a specialized evaluation procedure.
candidate-evaluation.noteTitle: Evaluation signal, extra feedback, and procedure are distinct
candidate-evaluation.noteCopy: The primary signal says how candidates compare or score. Extra feedback explains more about the result; procedure describes how the evaluation is carried out.

dimensions.title: Primary evaluation signal
dimensions.question: What is the main quality signal?

options.name: Scalar objective
options.description: Return one numeric value for each candidate.

options.name: Vector objective
options.description: Return several objective values that capture competing criteria.

options.name: Preference or ranking
options.description: Compare candidates pairwise or return an ordinal ranking when absolute scoring is difficult.

dimensions.note: Quality-diversity search can pair an objective value with a behavior descriptor to preserve niches.

dimensions.title: Additional evaluation feedback
dimensions.question: What else does the evaluator return?

options.name: Metadata
options.description: Attach structured outcomes such as correctness, exceptions, profiler data, or per-instance metrics.

options.name: Verbalized feedback
options.description: Summarize traces or outcomes as natural-language diagnosis that can guide revision.

dimensions.note: Additional feedback enriches the primary signal; it does not replace it by definition.

dimensions.title: Evaluation procedure
dimensions.question: How is evaluation carried out?

options.name: Staged
options.description: Screen candidates cheaply before promoting survivors to more expensive tests.

options.name: Approximate
options.description: Use proxy, partial, or reduced-fidelity measurements during search.

options.name: Parallel
options.description: Distribute candidate assessments across workers, devices, or environments.

options.name: Repeated
options.description: Aggregate repeated runs or scenarios to stabilize noisy measurements.

dimensions.note: Staged and approximate evaluation reduce cost in different ways; repetition targets measurement noise.

candidate-evaluation.flowNote: The evaluation procedure determines how signals are obtained, not which candidates are retained.

population-update.title: Population Update
population-update.lead: After evaluation, the system decides what enters or remains in the reusable search history. This layer concerns change over time, not the shape of the population or archive.
population-update.noteTitle: Update policy is orthogonal to population structure
population-update.noteCopy: The same structure can use different replacement rules, and the same replacement rule can operate on flat, island, or archive-based designs.

dimensions.title: Replacement mechanisms
dimensions.question: How are evaluated candidates retained?

options.name: Incremental insertion
options.description: Add candidates or trajectory records to a growing reusable pool; retrieval happens later.

options.name: Elitist replacement
options.description: Admit candidates that satisfy a top-k, elite, or descriptor-cell improvement criterion.

options.name: Generational replacement
options.description: Construct a new candidate batch and carry it forward as the next population.

dimensions.note: These update patterns govern temporal turnover and retention, not parent choice.

population-update.flowNote: Population update closes one iteration by deciding what future iterations can reuse.

exploration-exploitation.title: Explore–Exploit Control
exploration-exploitation.lead: Exploration seeks new search directions; exploitation develops promising ones. In LLM-guided evolutionary search, this balance emerges from or is shaped by several coupled choices across the loop.
exploration-exploitation.noteTitle: A control perspective across the system
exploration-exploitation.noteCopy: This is not a ninth chronological step. It is a global search strategy that interacts with parent selection, generation mechanisms, model choice, archives, and feedback.

dimensions.title: Implicit strategies
dimensions.question: Can the balance emerge without a dedicated controller?

options.name: Unified generation
options.description: Use one generation process and let stochastic proposals, archive diversity, and repeated refinement jointly produce exploratory and exploitative behavior.

options.name: Memory and sampling
options.description: Let archive structure, parent sampling, and retention distribute search pressure without an explicit explore/exploit mode switch.

dimensions.note: Representative systems: AlphaEvolve, ThetaEvolve, and EvoSLD.

dimensions.title: State-independent control
dimensions.question: Is search pressure fixed or scheduled in advance?

options.name: Fixed allocation or modes
options.description: Set the proportions or rules for exploratory and exploitative actions before the run; examples include RankEvolve and MadEvolve.

options.name: Preset stage schedule
options.description: Move through a hand-designed progression, often emphasizing broader exploration early and more conservative refinement later.

dimensions.note: Representative systems include RankEvolve, MadEvolve, and AgentLTV; the schedule is interpretable but cannot react to an individual run's trajectory.

dimensions.title: Adaptive control
dimensions.question: Does observed progress change the balance online?

options.name: Progress or uncertainty feedback
options.description: Adjust search intensity from recent improvement, stagnation, uncertainty, or strategy outcomes; AdaEvolve is one example.

options.name: Tree statistics or bandit rewards
options.description: Use visit statistics or reward estimates to allocate effort between broader exploration and deeper refinement.

dimensions.note: Representative systems include AdaEvolve, AgentLTV, SEA-TS, TIDE, and ShinkaEvolve; feedback adds responsiveness as well as controller complexity.

exploration-exploitation.flowNote: Implicit strategies distribute this balance across system design; fixed strategies prescribe it; adaptive strategies update it during search.
